prompt: `ls logs nosuchdir > out.txt` and the error still appears on screen. Why?
hint: The command wrote to two places and you redirected one of them.

choices.text: The redirection was applied after `ls` had already printed its error
choices.why: Redirection is set up before the program starts, which is why it works on every command.

choices.text: `ls` writes errors directly to the terminal device
choices.why: It writes to descriptor 2, which happens to be the terminal because nothing changed it.

choices.text: `>` redirects stdout; the error went to stderr
choices.why: Right — two streams, and `>` moves one of them.

choices.text: The directory does not exist, so the error had no destination
choices.why: The listing of `logs` was redirected successfully; the error is a separate stream.

prompt: `ls` printed five names across one line on screen and one per line into a file. What happened?
hint: Something asked a question about where its output was going.

choices.text: The file has no width, so `ls` used the longest possible line
choices.why: `ls` uses one per line for a file, which is the opposite of a long line.

choices.text: `ls` checks whether its output is a terminal
choices.why: Right — the `isatty()` question, and `grep` and `ps` do the same thing.

choices.text: The shell reformatted the output on its way to the file
choices.why: The shell connects descriptors; it does not touch the bytes.

choices.text: Columns are added by the terminal emulator, not by `ls`
choices.why: The terminal draws characters it is given; the spacing came from `ls`.

prompt: The descriptor number a program writes its error messages to: ____
hint: A single digit.

prompt: `ls nosuchdir 2>&1 > out.txt` leaves the error on screen and `out.txt` empty. Why?
hint: Read the two operators left to right, and ask what descriptor 1 was at each moment.

choices.text: `2>&1` is ignored when a `>` follows it on the same line
choices.why: Both are applied; the question is what each one saw when it ran.

choices.text: `out.txt` was truncated after the error was written to it
choices.why: The error was never written to the file; it went to the terminal.

choices.text: `2>&1` needs `&>`, which is the bash shorthand
choices.why: `2>&1` works on its own, in the other order.

choices.text: When `2>&1` ran, descriptor 1 was still the terminal
choices.why: Right — `2>&1` copies where 1 points at that moment, and `>` moved 1 afterwards.

prompt: `sort file.txt > file.txt` leaves the file empty. When did the data go?
hint: One of the two things happens before the other.

choices.text: The shell truncated the file before `sort` opened it
choices.why: Right — `>` empties the target first, so `sort` read an empty file.

choices.text: `sort` failed and wrote no output, leaving the original untouched
choices.why: The original is gone, which means something wrote to it.

choices.text: `sort` read the file into memory and crashed before writing
choices.why: It did not crash; it read nothing and wrote nothing, successfully.

choices.text: The shell buffered the output and lost it when `sort` exited
choices.why: There is no such buffer; output goes to the file as it is produced.

prompt: `some-command | grep error` finds nothing, but you can see the word `error` on your screen. What is happening?
hint: A pipe carries one stream.

choices.text: `grep` needs `-i`, because the message is capitalised
choices.why: Possible and easy to rule out, and it would not explain a message you can see clearly.

choices.text: The command buffers its output, so `grep` sees it late
choices.why: Buffering delays output; it does not make `grep` miss it.

choices.text: It is on stderr, which a bare `|` does not carry
choices.why: Right — `2>&1 |` is the form that searches both.

choices.text: `grep` reads just the first line of a pipe without `-a`
choices.why: `grep` reads the whole stream; `-a` is about binary files.

prompt: Write a command's output to a root-owned file from a pipeline, since your shell cannot: `some-command | sudo ____ /root/out.txt`
hint: Three letters.

prompt: `grep pattern huge.log | head -5` returns instantly on a ten-gigabyte file. Why?
hint: Two programs run at the same time, and one of them stops early.

choices.text: `grep` reads the file backwards, so the first hits come first
choices.why: `grep` reads forwards; the early return is about the other end of the pipe.

choices.text: `head` exits after five lines and SIGPIPE ends `grep`
choices.why: Right — section 93's signal, with the whole pipeline finishing before `grep` is done.

choices.text: The shell runs `head` first and afterwards starts `grep`
choices.why: Both start together; that is what a pipe is.

choices.text: `grep` counts matches and stops when `head` has enough
choices.why: `grep` has no idea how many `head` wants; the kernel ends it.

prompt:
Two pipelines give the same answer. Which is better, and why?

```
sort access.log | cut -d" " -f9 | uniq -c
cut -d" " -f9 access.log | sort | uniq -c
```
hint: One of them sorts a hundred and fifty characters per line and the other sorts three.

choices.text: The first, because sorting whole lines groups related requests
choices.why: Grouping by whole line is not what the question asks for, and it costs more.

choices.text: Neither; they do identical work in a different order
choices.why: The work differs: one sorts long lines and the other sorts short fields.

choices.text: The second, because `cut` throws away most of each line first
choices.why: Right — reduce before you sort, and on a large log that is minutes.

choices.text: The first, because `sort` is faster on its original input order
choices.why: Input order does not change what `sort` has to compare.

prompt: Complete the pipeline that answers "which status codes, and how many of each": `cut -d" " -f9 access.log | sort | ____ -c | sort -rn`
hint: Four letters.

prompt: You want everything in a CSV except the header line. Which command?
hint: One of these counts from the top and the rest count from the bottom.

choices.text: `tail -2 f.csv`, taking the last two lines
choices.why: That gives the last two lines, which is the opposite end.

choices.text: `head -n -1 file.csv`
choices.why: That drops the *last* line, and the header is the first.

choices.text: `tail -n 2 file.csv`
choices.why: The same as `tail -2`; the plus sign is what changes the meaning.

choices.text: `tail -n +2 f.csv`
choices.why: Right — the `+` means "from line 2 to the end".

prompt: A config file will not parse and every line looks correct. Which command shows you why?
hint: The problem is something you cannot see.

choices.text: `cat -A file`
choices.why: Right — it shows tabs as `^I`, line ends as `$` and carriage returns as `^M`.

choices.text: `cat -n file`
choices.why: Numbering the lines helps you report the problem and not find it.

choices.text: `wc -L file`
choices.why: The longest line's length rarely explains a parse failure.

choices.text: `file file`
choices.why: It reports the file's type, which is already known to be text.

prompt: Watch a log as it grows, in a pager you can scroll back in when you stop: `____ +F app.log`
hint: Four letters, and it is the pager `man` uses.

prompt: `grep -c o` on the single line `hello world` prints `1`. Why not `2`?
hint: Read what the flag counts.

choices.text: The second `o` is in a different word, and `grep` counts per word
choices.why: `grep` has no idea what a word is unless you ask with `-w`.

choices.text: `-c` counts matching lines, and there is one line
choices.why: Right — `grep -o | wc -l` is the way to count occurrences.

choices.text: `grep` stops reading a line after the first match
choices.why: It stops looking on that line, which is why `-c` is a line count — but the count is the point.

choices.text: Two matches on one line are collapsed into one by default
choices.why: Nothing is collapsed; `-o` prints both.

prompt: You are searching a log for the IP address `10.0.1.5`. Which is safest?
hint: One of these turns the pattern language off.

choices.text: `grep 10.0.1.5 access.log`
choices.why: The dots are wildcards, so this also matches `10x0y1z5` if such a string existed.

choices.text: `grep -E '10.0.1.5' access.log`
choices.why: The same problem: `-E` does not make a dot literal.

choices.text: `grep -w 10.0.1.5 access.log`
choices.why: `-w` fixes word boundaries and leaves the dots as wildcards.

choices.text: `grep -F 10.0.1.5 access.log`
choices.why: Right — `-F` means no pattern language, so a dot is a dot.

prompt: A script under `set -e` stops at a `grep` that found nothing. Is that a bug in the script?
hint: Section 99 said what a non-zero status means, and what `grep` means by 1.

choices.text: Yes — `grep` should exit 0 when it ran successfully
choices.why: Its exit status is deliberately the answer to the question, not a report on whether it ran.

choices.text: No — `grep` failing means the file could not be read
choices.why: That is status 2; 1 is a clean search that matched nothing.

choices.text: In effect yes: no match is normal, so wrap it in an `if`
choices.why: Right — `if grep -q …; then` or `|| true`, depending on what you meant.

choices.text: No — `set -e` does not act on the last command of a pipeline
choices.why: It does; the exemptions are conditions and `&&`/`||` chains.

prompt: Match each `grep` flag to what it does.
hint: Six flags, and one of them inverts the whole question.

pairs.right: print the lines that do not match
print each match on its own line
print only the names of files that matched
print nothing; the exit status is the answer
also print two lines after each match

prompt: Count how many times the word `GET` appears in a log, not how many lines contain it: `grep ____ GET access.log | wc -l`
hint: One short flag, and it prints each match on its own line.

prompt: Why does `grep -E "c[^o]t"` not match the line `ct`?
hint: Ask how many characters the pattern describes.

choices.text: `[^o]` is a character that is not `o`; `ct` has none
choices.why: Right — negation is still one character, not zero.

choices.text: `[^o]` matches only letters, and there is nothing to match
choices.why: It matches any single character except `o`, letter or not.

choices.text: `^` inside brackets anchors to the start of the line
choices.why: Inside brackets `^` is negation; the anchor meaning is outside them.

choices.text: `grep -E` requires at least three characters in a pattern
choices.why: Patterns can be one character long.

prompt: `grep -oE '".*"'` on a line with two quoted strings returns one long match. Why, and what is the fix?
hint: Quantifiers take as much as they can.

choices.text: `grep` matched the longest line; use `-m1` to stop at the first
choices.why: `-m1` limits how many lines are printed, not how much of one line matches.

choices.text: `.*` is greedy, so it runs to the last quote; use `[^"]*`
choices.why: Right — "anything except the delimiter" is what you meant, and grep has no lazy quantifier.

choices.text: `-o` concatenates adjacent matches; use `-oE` with `-w`
choices.why: `-o` prints matches separately; the two were one match.

choices.text: The quotes need escaping; use `\"` on both ends
choices.why: A quote is not special in a regex, so escaping it changes nothing.

prompt: Match a line that is exactly four digits, a dash, two digits, a dash and two digits, and nothing else: `grep -E "____[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$"`
hint: One character: the anchor for the start of a line.

prompt: `cut -d, -f5,2 data.csv` prints field 2 before field 5. How do you get them the other way round?
hint: One of the tools in this lesson prints fields in the order you wrote.

choices.text: `cut -d, -f5 -f2 data.csv`
choices.why: Repeating `-f` does not change the order; `cut` still outputs in file order.

choices.text: `cut -d, --output-order=5,2 data.csv`
choices.why: There is no such option; `cut` has no way to reorder.

choices.text: `awk -F, '{print $5, $2}' data.csv`
choices.why: Right — `awk` prints the fields in the order you name them.

choices.text: `cut -d, -f5,2 data.csv | sort -t, -k2`
choices.why: Sorting reorders rows, not the columns within a row.

prompt: A file's columns are separated by runs of spaces of different widths. What makes `cut -d" "` work on it?
hint: The delimiter has to become exactly one character wide.

choices.text: `tr -s " "` first, squeezing runs to one space
choices.why: Right, and `awk` is the alternative, since it splits on runs by default.

choices.text: `cut -d"  "` with two spaces in the delimiter
choices.why: `-d` takes a single character; two is an error.

choices.text: `cut --whitespace`, which treats runs as one
choices.why: No such option exists.

choices.text: `sed 's/ //g'` first, to remove the spaces entirely
choices.why: That removes the separators entirely and joins the columns together.

prompt: Take every field from the third to the end of the line: `cut -d, -f____ data.csv`
hint: A digit and one character.

prompt: `sort` on the numbers 26, 31, 109, 113 puts 109 first. What is wrong?
hint: It is doing exactly what it was asked.

choices.text: The numbers have different widths and need padding to line up
choices.why: Padding would fix it and the flag is simpler and does not change the data.

choices.text: `sort` needs `-u` to compare values rather than lines
choices.why: `-u` drops duplicates; it has nothing to do with the comparison.

choices.text: The file has trailing whitespace, which sorts before digits
choices.why: Possible in general, and here the order is exactly what alphabetical gives.

choices.text: That is alphabetical order; it needs `-n`
choices.why: Right — `1` sorts before `2`, correctly, on text that happens to be numbers.

prompt: `sort -t, -k5` sorts by more than field 5. What does `-k5` actually mean?
hint: A key is a range, and you gave one end of it.

choices.text: Field 5, plus any field that ties with it
choices.why: Ties are broken by the whole line unless you say otherwise, which is a different rule.

choices.text: From field 5 onward, to the end of the line
choices.why: Right — `-k5,5` is the way to say field 5 alone.

choices.text: Each field up to and including 5
choices.why: The range runs the other way, from the named field onwards.

choices.text: Field 5, unless it is empty, in which case field 6
choices.why: `sort` does not fall through to the next field.

prompt: Sort `du -h` output so that `2.5M` comes before `1G`: `du -h | sort ____`
hint: One short flag, and it is not `-n`.

prompt:
`printf "a
a
b
a
" | uniq` prints three lines. Why not two?
hint: The name promises more than the command does.

choices.text: `uniq` keeps the first and the last occurrence of a value
choices.why: It keeps one per *run*, and there were three runs here.

choices.text: `uniq` needs `-u` to remove duplicates
choices.why: `-u` keeps values that appear exactly once, which is a different thing again.

choices.text: It collapses adjacent duplicates; the last `a` was not
choices.why: Right — sort first, always.

choices.text: `uniq` compares whole lines including trailing whitespace
choices.why: It does, and these lines are identical; adjacency is what separated them.

prompt: A pipeline reports `5 /` three times in its top four results. What went wrong?
hint: The counts are small and the same value appears more than once.

choices.text: `uniq -c` ran on unsorted input and counted runs
choices.why: Right — each scattered group of five was counted separately.

choices.text: `sort -rn` compared the counts as text, so the order is wrong
choices.why: That would misorder the lines; it would not produce the same path three times.

choices.text: `cut` took the wrong field, so the paths are from another column
choices.why: The paths are real; the counts are what is wrong.

choices.text: The log genuinely contains three different paths that print the same
choices.why: They are identical strings; nothing renders them the same by accident.

prompt: Find the values that appear more than once in a sorted list: `sort ids.txt | uniq ____`
hint: One short flag.

prompt: `wc -l` says 0 and `grep -c .` says 1 on the same one-line file. Which is right?
hint: They count different things, and the file is missing something.

choices.text: `wc -l`, since a file with no newline has no complete line
choices.why: That is a defensible reading and it is not the only one; both answers are correct.

choices.text: Both: one counts newlines, the other non-empty lines
choices.why: Right — and the file has text with no newline at the end.

choices.text: `grep -c .`, since `wc -l` struggles with a file lacking a newline
choices.why: `wc` read it fine; it counted the newlines it found, which was none.

choices.text: Neither; the file is corrupt and should be rewritten
choices.why: A file with no trailing newline is common and perfectly valid.

prompt: How many *different* addresses are in a log?
hint: Two of these count lines and one counts values.

choices.text: `wc -l a.log`, which counts the requests
choices.why: That counts requests, which is a much larger number.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f1 a.log | wc -l`, repeats included
choices.why: That counts the addresses, including every repeat of each one.

choices.text: `grep -c "^10\." a.log`, for one prefix
choices.why: That counts one prefix, and counts repeats.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f1 a.log | sort -u | wc -l`
choices.why: Right — `sort -u` collapses repeats, so the count is of distinct values.

prompt: `echo "cat attack" | tr cat dog` prints `dog oggodk`. What did `tr` actually do?
hint: It has no idea what a word is.

choices.text: It replaced the first occurrence of `cat` and mangled the rest
choices.why: It never looked for `cat` at all; it looked for the letters separately.

choices.text: It matched `cat` case-insensitively and over-applied the result
choices.why: Case had nothing to do with it; all the text was lowercase.

choices.text: It mapped `c` to `d`, `a` to `o` and `t` to `g`, everywhere
choices.why: Right — three character-for-character substitutions, applied to every letter.

choices.text: It treated `dog` as a pattern and `cat` as the replacement
choices.why: The order is source then destination, and it is not a pattern either way.

prompt: Strip the carriage returns from a file that came from Windows: `tr ____ '\r' < windows.txt > unix.txt`
hint: One short flag.

prompt: `sed "s/cat/dog/"` on `the cat sat on the cat` leaves the second `cat`. Why?
hint: One letter is missing from the command.

choices.text: `sed` stops at the first match to avoid overlapping replacements
choices.why: Overlap is not the reason; the flag simply was not given.

choices.text: Substitution replaces the first match per line unless `g` is given
choices.why: Right — and `g` is not the default, which surprises everybody once.

choices.text: The second `cat` is at the end of the line, where `$` would be needed
choices.why: Position does not matter; the same thing happens mid-line.

choices.text: `sed` needs `-E` for a pattern to match more than once
choices.why: `-E` changes the pattern syntax, not how many replacements happen.

prompt: You are replacing `/usr/local` with `/opt` in a file. Which command is readable?
hint: The separator is whatever character follows the `s`.

choices.text: `sed 's/\/usr\/local/\/opt/'`
choices.why: That works and nobody can check it by eye, which is the point of the alternative.

choices.text: `sed 's/usr.local/opt/'`
choices.why: The unescaped dots are wildcards and the leading slash is gone.

choices.text: `sed -F 's:/usr/local:/opt:'`
choices.why: `sed` has no `-F`; that flag belongs to `grep`.

choices.text: `sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|'`
choices.why: Right — a different separator, and no escaping at all.

prompt: What does `sed -n '2,4p'` print, and what would `sed '2,4p'` print instead?
hint: One flag turns off something that happens by default.

choices.text: Lines 2 to 4; without `-n`, every line with 2 to 4 repeated
choices.why: Right — `-n` suppresses the automatic printing that `p` then re-enables selectively.

choices.text: Lines 2 to 4 in both cases; `-n` only affects the exit status
choices.why: `-n` changes the output, which is its whole purpose.

choices.text: Lines 2 to 4; without `-n`, nothing, because `p` needs `-n`
choices.why: `p` works either way; `-n` decides whether everything else is printed too.

choices.text: Nothing; `-n` and `p` cancel out and `2,4p` prints lines 2 to 4
choices.why: The pairing is the other way round: `-n` plus `p` is the selective form.

prompt: Edit a file in place and keep a copy of the original: `sed ____ 's/old/new/g' config.txt`
hint: Two characters, a dot, and three more.

prompt: Why can `awk '$9 >= 400'` do something `grep` cannot?
hint: One of them compares numbers and the other compares shapes.

choices.text: `awk` reads the whole file into memory and `grep` streams it
choices.why: Both stream; neither loads the file.

choices.text: `awk` understands the log format and `grep` does not
choices.why: Neither knows anything about logs; one was told which field to look at.

choices.text: Arithmetic on a named field, not a text pattern
choices.why: Right — `grep` would have to describe the shape of a number and would catch others.

choices.text: `grep` struggles with three-digit numbers unless `-E` is used
choices.why: It can, with or without `-E`; matching is not the limitation.

prompt: `awk '{print NF}' access.log | sort -u` prints 12, 15, 18 and 20. What does that tell you?
hint: Every line looks the same shape and four different counts came back.

choices.text: The file is corrupt and some lines are truncated
choices.why: The lines are complete; something in them has a variable number of spaces.

choices.text: `awk` is miscounting because the delimiter was not set
choices.why: The default splitting on whitespace is what produced these counts, correctly.

choices.text: Four different log formats were concatenated into one file
choices.why: One format, with a free-text field in it, produces this on its own.

choices.text: A field holds spaces, so later positional fields drift
choices.why: Right — the quoted user-agent, and `$NF` still works because it counts backwards.

prompt: What does `awk '{c[$7]++} END {for (p in c) print c[p], p}'` do?
hint: The array is subscripted by a string.

choices.text: Counts each distinct value of field 7
choices.why: Right — the same answer as `sort | uniq -c`, in one pass and without sorting.

choices.text: Prints field 7 of each line, numbered
choices.why: The number is a count per distinct value, not a line number.

choices.text: Sums field 7 across the file and prints the total
choices.why: `++` counts occurrences; summing would be `+= $7`.

choices.text: Prints the seventh field of just the last line
choices.why: The `END` block runs once, and the loop walks every key the body collected.

prompt: Match each awk variable or block to what it is.
hint: Four pieces, two of them variables and two of them blocks that run once.

pairs.right: the line number you are on
how many fields this line has
runs once, before the first line
runs once, after the last line

prompt: Sum the fifth column of a CSV, skipping the header, in one command: `awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$5} ____ {print s}' sales.csv`
hint: Three letters, uppercase.

prompt: You have two sorted lists of usernames and want the ones in the first that are not in the second. Which command?
hint: The numbers suppress columns rather than select them.

choices.text: `comm -12 a.txt b.txt`
choices.why: Suppressing 1 and 2 leaves the third column, which is the ones in both.

choices.text: `comm -23 a.txt b.txt`
choices.why: Right — suppress columns 2 and 3, leaving only what is in the first file.

choices.text: `comm -13 a.txt b.txt`
choices.why: That leaves the second column: only in the second file.

choices.text: `diff a.txt b.txt`
choices.why: That reports changes by position, which is a different question.

prompt: Two files contain the same lines in a different order. What do `comm -12` and `diff` say?
hint: One of them cares where a line is.

choices.text: Both say they are the same, since the contents match
choices.why: `diff` compares line by line in order, so a reordering is a long list of changes.

choices.text: Both say they differ, since the files are not byte-identical
choices.why: `comm` compares membership on sorted input and finds every line in both.

choices.text: `comm -12` lists every line; `diff` reports many changes
choices.why: Right — membership against position, which is the whole difference between them.

choices.text: `comm -12` prints nothing; `diff` prints nothing
choices.why: Neither is silent: one finds everything in common, the other finds differences.

prompt: Turn a column of values into one comma-separated line: `cut -d, -f2 sales.csv | paste ____
hint: A dash, one letter, one more letter and a comma.

prompt: `find . -type f | xargs wc -l` reports `./a: No such file or directory`. What happened?
hint: One of the filenames has something in it that `xargs` treats as a separator.

choices.text: `find` printed a relative path that `wc` could not resolve
choices.why: `wc` resolved `./plain.txt` in the same run, from the same directory.

choices.text: `xargs` ran out of command-line space and split the list badly
choices.why: Splitting on the length limit happens between arguments, never inside one.

choices.text: `wc` struggles with a file whose name begins with a dot-slash
choices.why: It read `./plain.txt` in the same command.

choices.text: A filename holds a space, and `xargs` split it in two
choices.why: Right — `find -print0 | xargs -0` is the fix, and it is the form to type by default.

prompt: `find . -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm` found nothing. Why is that still dangerous?
hint: Think about what the command is run with when the list is empty.

choices.text: `rm` with no arguments deletes the current directory
choices.why: It refuses and prints usage; the danger is a command that does something instead.

choices.text: `xargs` runs the command once anyway, with no arguments
choices.why: Right — harmless for `rm`, and `ls` would have listed everything as if it were a result.

choices.text: `find` prints an error that `rm` reads as a filename
choices.why: `find`'s errors go to stderr, which the pipe does not carry.

choices.text: `xargs` waits for input from the terminal when the pipe is empty
choices.why: It reads the pipe to end-of-file and then runs; it does not fall back to the terminal.

prompt: Make a `find` and `xargs` pipeline safe for filenames containing spaces: `find . -type f ____ | xargs -0 wc -l`
hint: Two words after the dash, joined by nothing.

prompt: Put this pipeline's stages in the order that does the least work.
trap: Throw lines away, then narrow to one field, then group, then count, then order.

prompt: Which pipeline answers "the ten busiest paths" correctly?
hint: One stage in this pipeline is not optional.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f7 a.log | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10`
choices.why: Without a sort first, `uniq -c` counts runs and every number is wrong.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f7 a.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`
choices.why: Right — group, count, order by count.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f7 a.log | sort -rn | uniq -c | head`
choices.why: Sorting paths numerically does nothing, and `uniq -c` then counts before ordering.

choices.text: `sort -u a.log | cut -d" " -f7 | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`
choices.why: Sorting whole lines does not group equal paths together, and nothing orders by count.

prompt: A log line ends with a response time in milliseconds. How do you find the slow requests?
hint: The user-agent field has spaces in it, so counting fields from the left is unsafe.

choices.text: `awk '$NF > 3000' access.log`
choices.why: Right — `$NF` counts from the end, past the variable-width user agent.

choices.text: `awk '$12 > 3000' access.log`
choices.why: The field number varies line to line, because of the quoted user agent.

choices.text: `grep -E ' [0-9]{4,}$' access.log`
choices.why: That finds four-digit numbers at the end, which is close and also catches 1000 to 2999.

choices.text: `cut -d" " -f12 access.log | sort -rn | head`
choices.why: Same problem as the second, plus it loses the rest of the line.

prompt: Match each question to the tool that answers it.
hint: Six questions, six tools, and three of them sound like they overlap.

prompt: A script writes a log with `some-command > app.log` and the errors are missing from it. What is the fix?
hint: A pipe and a redirect both carry one stream by default.

choices.text: `some-command | tee app.log`
choices.why: That copies stdout to the file and the screen, and still leaves stderr out.

choices.text: `some-command 2>&1 > app.log`, the other way round
choices.why: That is the order that does not work: 2 is copied while 1 is still the terminal.

choices.text: `some-command > app.log 2>&1` in that order
choices.why: Right — point 1 at the file first, then make 2 a copy of 1.

choices.text: `some-command 2> app.log`
choices.why: That captures the errors and loses the output the script was writing.

prompt: You need to replace a path in fifty config files. What do you do first?
hint: There is no undo, and there is a way to look before you leap.

choices.text: Back up the whole directory with `cp -r`
choices.why: Sensible and slower than the thing that shows you the change before making it.

choices.text: Run `sed -i` on one file and check the result
choices.why: Better than nothing, and it has already changed a file you may have to restore.

choices.text: Use `-i.bak` so each file keeps a copy
choices.why: Worth doing as well, and it still applies the change before you have seen it.

choices.text: Run the `sed` without `-i` and read it
choices.why: Right — it changes nothing, costs a second, and shows what the pattern really matched.

prompt: Which of these silently give a wrong answer rather than an error?
hint: Four failures from this lesson; two of them announce themselves.

choices.text: `uniq -c` on unsorted input
choices.why: Yes — it counts runs and prints plausible small numbers.

choices.text: `sort` on numbers without `-n`
choices.why: Yes — the output looks sorted and 109 is before 26.

choices.text: `2>&1 > file` instead of `> file 2>&1`
choices.why: Yes — a file is written and the errors are not in it.

choices.text: `cut -d", "` with a two-character delimiter
choices.why: `cut` refuses: the delimiter must be a single character.

choices.text: `join` on unsorted input
choices.why: Yes — unlike `comm`, it does not complain.

prompt: Put the steps of investigating an unfamiliar file in order.
items: run it on the whole file
trap: See a line, see how much there is, check every line is that shape, test small, then run.

prompt: Count the distinct values in the first column of a log, in one pipeline: `cut -d" " -f1 a.log | sort ____ | wc -l`
hint: One short flag, and it drops duplicates.

prompt: Make a pipeline report a failure in any stage, not just the last: `set -o ____`
hint: One word, eight letters.

prompt: Make a command read a file as its standard input, without naming the file to the command: `wc -l ____ app.log`
hint: One character.

prompt: Read every stage's exit status after a pipeline, not just the last: `echo "${____[@]}"`
hint: One word in capitals, eleven letters.

prompt: Show the first forty bytes of a file rather than the first forty lines: `head ____ 40 access.log`
hint: A dash and one letter.

prompt: Match a line containing two or more consecutive `a` characters and nothing else: `grep -E "^a{____}$"`
hint: A digit and a comma.

prompt: Drop a CSV's header before cutting a column: `____ -n +2 sales.csv | cut -d, -f5`
hint: Four letters.

prompt: Sort by field 5 alone, rather than from field 5 to the end of the line: `sort -t, ____ -rn sales.csv`
hint: Two characters, a digit, a comma and the same digit.

prompt: Show the most common values and how many times each appeared: `sort f.txt | uniq ____ | sort -rn`
hint: A dash and one letter.

prompt: Count only the lines of a file, not its words and bytes: `wc ____ access.log`
hint: A dash and one letter.

prompt: `wc -c` and `wc -m` disagree on a file of Portuguese text. Why?
hint: One counts storage and the other counts text.

choices.text: The file has a byte-order mark that `-m` skips
choices.why: A BOM would be a three-byte difference; the gap here is proportional to the accents.

choices.text: `-m` excludes the newline at the end of each line
choices.why: Both count newlines; they are one byte and one character each.

choices.text: An accented character is one character and two bytes
choices.why: Right — `ã` is two bytes, so bytes exceed characters.

choices.text: `-c` counts the file's blocks on disk rather than its bytes
choices.why: `-c` is bytes; block usage is what `du` reports.

prompt: Which job is `tr` the right tool for?
hint: It works on characters and has no pattern language.

choices.text: Replacing the word `staging` with `production` in a config
choices.why: That is a word, and `tr` would map each letter separately.

choices.text: Turning a comma-separated line into one value per line
choices.why: Right — `tr , '\n'` is the shortest way to say it.

choices.text: Printing just the lines that contain an error
choices.why: `tr` has no idea what a line is; that is `grep`.

choices.text: Summing the numbers in the third column
choices.why: That is arithmetic on a field, which is `awk`.

prompt: Replace every occurrence on each line, not just the first: `sed 's/old/new/____'`
hint: One letter.

prompt: Print the last field of every line, whatever the field count: `awk '{print $____}'`
hint: Two letters, uppercase.

prompt: Print the lines that are in both of two sorted files: `comm ____ a.txt b.txt`
hint: A dash and two digits.

prompt: Run the command once per input line instead of packing many onto one command line: `xargs ____ gzip`
hint: A dash, one letter and a digit.

prompt: You want every line of a log that is not a health check. Which flag?
hint: The question is the inverse of what grep normally does.

choices.text: `grep -c health`, counting the matches
choices.why: That counts them rather than removing them.

choices.text: `grep -l health`
choices.why: That names the files, which you already know.

choices.text: `grep -o health`
choices.why: That prints the matched word, repeatedly.

choices.text: `grep -v health`, inverted
choices.why: Right — invert the match, and chain it for each thing you want gone.

prompt: Which of these commands changes a file?
hint: Three of the four print to standard output and stop there.

choices.text: `grep pattern file`
choices.why: It prints matching lines and leaves the file alone.

choices.text: `awk '{print $1}' file`
choices.why: It prints a column and leaves the file alone.

choices.text: `sed -i 's/a/b/' file`
choices.why: Right — `-i` is the flag that edits in place, with no undo.

choices.text: `sort -n file`
choices.why: It prints the sorted lines; the file is unchanged.

prompt: A one-liner has grown to three awk conditions and four variables. What now?
hint: The lesson's closing said where the line is.

choices.text: Split it into two awk commands joined by a pipe
choices.why: That works and leaves the same amount of logic spread across two places.

choices.text: Write it as a script in a file
choices.why: Right — it has become a program, and a program belongs in a file with a name.

choices.text: Move it into a shell alias so it is easier to reuse
choices.why: An alias makes an unreadable line easier to rerun and no easier to change.

choices.text: Rewrite it in `sed`, which handles multiple commands
choices.why: `sed` is less capable here, not more; that direction goes backwards.

prompt: Send both a command's output and its errors to the same file: `some-command > log.txt ____`
hint: Four characters.

prompt: Count how many distinct status codes appear in a log: `cut -d" " -f9 a.log | ____ | wc -l`
hint: Two words: a command and one short flag.

prompt: Squeeze runs of spaces into one, so `cut -d" "` works on padded text: `tr ____ " "`
hint: A dash and one letter.
